prize_parts.citation: for showing how technological change and international trade reshape labour demand, wages and local labour markets

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1 (B027, Autor, Hanson, Katz, one part). My alternatives have changed: B006 replaces B001. The case still rests on substance. The achievement answers a first-order question, who gains and loses when technology and import competition change labour demand. It pairs a conceptual account (skill demand and supply, the race between education and technology, tasks) with transparent local labour-market evidence. The findings have been replicated, extended and contested for a decade or more. Critiques have mostly refined the magnitude, persistence and external validity of the China-shock effects, and they have not removed the finding that adjustment is slow, geographically concentrated and costly. As a macroeconomist, the link between that micro evidence on reallocation and aggregate adjustment is what I value most. On the chair's question about Katz, I see his distinct contribution as the supply-and-demand account of the skill premium and its later extension to computerisation, polarisation and the education-technology race. That work supplies the long-run framework in which the trade-shock evidence is read. It is separate from his role in the mobility work in B028, and separate from the formal task-model contributions of Acemoglu, Levy and Murnane. This is why I would word the citation around labour demand, wages and local labour markets, not around the task model as theory, which limits the overlap with 2023 and 2024. If the committee instead narrows the achievement to import competition and local adjustment, I would accept Autor, Dorn and Hanson, with a citation such as 'for showing how import competition reshapes local labour markets, employment and wages'. I would prefer that to the two-name Autor-Hanson fallback, because Dorn is a co-originator of the central papers. I regard the choice between the two trios as a decision on the scope of the citation, not as a disagreement about merit.
statement.case_against: Attribution under the three-name cap is still the weakest point. Dorn is a central co-author of the trade-shock papers and is excluded, so half of the citation is credited less cleanly than it could be. Katz's skill-demand strand and the China-shock strand have different identification strategies and different co-authors, so a committee could reasonably see two prize-sized achievements joined by Autor. Credit for the task framework extends beyond the credited names, to Acemoglu (2024), Levy and Murnane, and the Katz-Murphy lineage. Goldin (2023) and Card (2021) are adjacent. The size, persistence and external validity of the China-shock effects remain debated, and the local designs need more structure to support aggregate welfare claims. I have also lowered B001 as an alternative. My opening first place for Mian and Sufi was premature on maturity, since the credit-supply and expectations debate has not settled.

responses.point: Friberg's round-1 file moved to Autor, Hanson and Katz. He argues that a trade-shock-only trio would credit one half of the achievement, and that the citation should be worded around findings on labour demand, wages and local labour markets to limit overlap with the task literature. He still counts Dorn's omission as a real cost.
responses.response: I agree on both the logic and the wording. The credited work has to match what the citation claims, and a joint technology-and-trade citation needs the skill-demand anchor. I would add one commitment that you and I have left implicit. If the committee cannot defend the joint scope, we should switch to Autor, Dorn and Hanson with a citation limited to import competition. We should not keep the broad citation and quietly drop the strand that supports it. I also share your view that Dorn's exclusion under the cap is a cost and not a clean outcome, and I would not describe the trio as uniquely correct.

responses.point: Hassler prefers B006 with Kiyotaki and Moore only. He regards collateral amplification as a foundational mechanism with clean attribution, and he argues that Gertler should stay out because the accelerator lineage overlaps with the 2022 prize. He admits that the contribution is mainly theoretical and that B027 has a broader empirical base.
responses.response: I agree that a Kiyotaki-Moore pair is the cleanest attribution on the shortlist, and I have moved B006 into my alternatives, replacing B001. I do not think weaker direct identification disqualifies it. It is a reason to weigh it behind evidence that has been tested directly in many settings. The citation question you raise is fair. A statement that Kiyotaki and Moore explain how asset-price feedback turns temporary shocks into persistent credit cycles is distinct from bank runs and intermediation. I would still want the committee to say explicitly why Gertler is not credited. My ranking rests on weighing broad, tested empirical content against a clean theoretical originator pair, and I do not think the scientific standing of B006 is in doubt.

responses.point: Krusell's round-1 file moved from B012 to B027 with Autor, Hanson and Katz. He argues that Katz is needed to cover both the technology and the trade strands, and that B012 has more crowded credit (Bernard, Eaton, Jensen, Kortum) and sits close to the 2008 prize. He still lists the 2023 and 2024 prizes and the persistence of the China shock as open points.
responses.response: I agree with the move, and I take your account of B012 seriously. I keep B012 as a first alternative because Helpman and Melitz are the clear originators of the heterogeneous-firm framework and a two-person award is clean. The unresolved credit to the Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum empirical and quantitative precursors, and the closeness to Krugman's 2008 prize, are the reasons it is not first for me. On persistence, I would rest the citation on the finding that adjustment is slow and geographically concentrated, which has survived reanalysis. I would not rest it on a particular effect size, which is where the critiques bite hardest.

responses.point: Teorell supports Autor, Katz and Hanson. He says he would support Autor, Dorn and Hanson if the committee narrows the citation to trade exposure, and he proposes wording the citation around the empirical demonstration of labour-market effects, not the task model. He also says B001 is only his first alternative to B012 if the committee wants a macro-finance award.
responses.response: Your conditional support is the position I hold too, and it should be put to the committee as an explicit choice of scope. I would also treat the two-prizes concern as a test of the citation text and not as a verdict on merit. If a single sentence on labour demand, wages and local labour markets covers what the Autor, Hanson and Katz papers show, the joint scope holds. If it needs two clauses with different authors, the narrower trio is the honest choice. On B001, I now agree with you and others that the credit-supply versus expectations debate is not settled, and I have moved it out of my alternatives for that reason.

uncertainties: Whether the committee reads the technology-and-skills strand and the China-shock strand as one achievement or two. This decides between Autor-Hanson-Katz and Autor-Dorn-Hanson, and I regard the choice as a close call.

How much the 2021, 2023 and 2024 labour, education and technology prizes reduce the marginal case for B027, and how cleanly the Autor-Katz skills framework can be separated from Acemoglu's task theory.

Which China-shock findings will hold up under continued reanalysis. I rely on persistent and geographically concentrated adjustment, and I am less sure about the long-run magnitudes and their external validity beyond the US episode.

Whether B006 (a clean theoretical originator pair) or B012 should be preferred over B027 if no coherent B027 citation can be agreed. I rank B012 first and B006 second among alternatives, and I hold this ordering with low confidence.
My reading relies on my own knowledge of the literature and the supplied files. I have not independently verified any claim.
statement.conflict_note: Updated disclosure. I am a long-time collaborator of Peter Klenow (credited in B017, not in my configuration or alternatives), and I have worked with Philippe Aghion and Antonin Bergeaud. My own research on creative destruction is adjacent to the 2025 prize themes, and I co-authored a summary of the 2025 prize, which I note for transparency. It is not part of B027 or my alternatives. I am a frequent co-author of Per Krusell and a co-author of John Hassler, both committee colleagues and IIES colleagues. None of these ties involves a credited name in B027, B012 or B006, so no recusal is apparent for my configuration. This is disclosed, not adjudicated.
